I run operations at the joint venture in Houston, and last Friday was the worst day of my quarter. The container from Pittsburgh missed the cut-off by four hours. Four hours. If it had left on Friday, our customers would have their valves today, and I would not be on the phone every morning apologizing. Instead, we have a shortfall of two hundred units, and the knock-on effect is everywhere. One customer has already stopped his own production line. In hindsight, we made a mistake too. We did not keep any buffer stock in the warehouse. If we had kept even fifty units, we would be in a much better position now. So this week I am asking the supplier for a rush order, and I am not paying a surcharge for it.

When the supplier called me about the delay, my first idea was to cancel the whole contract. I did not do it, and I am glad. If I were a younger manager, I would have made that call in anger. Instead, I looked at what we had. The penalty clause gave us a bargaining chip, and we used it carefully. We told them that if we were not long-term partners, we would have cancelled already. Then we asked for something useful. They agreed to a rush order with no surcharge, and the two items on backorder will ship by air at their cost. In the end, we did not use the penalty at all. Goodwill is cheap to keep and very expensive to rebuild. The only deal-breaker for me now would be a second delay without a phone call.

First, you check the size of the shortfall and the knock-on effect on your customers. Then, you read the contract to see if there is a penalty clause. After that, you call the supplier and explain what the delay costs you today. Next, you ask for a rush order without a surcharge. Finally, you write down what was agreed, including the items on backorder.
